consensus_summary: Consensus primary symbolic reading is the inward/true Jew (heart circumcised by the Spirit, authentic covenant membership), drawn chiefly from Rom 2:28-29 and related texts; ordinary sense remains literal ethnic/national identity, with no settled single symbolic meaning. Common alternatives include church-as-spiritual-Israel/supersession, Johannine opposition symbol, faithful remnant within ethnic Israel, and (minority) legalism/unbelief polemic.
book_summary: One belonging to Judah, used at several scales: the tribe itself, Israel collectively, the ethnic people, or the faithful inward subset whose praise comes from God; context determines the sense.
consensus_core_identification: Inward/spiritual true covenant member (Rom 2:28-29) as the chief symbolic sense, distinct from ordinary ethnic referent
book_core_identification: One belonging to Judah, scaled by context from tribe/Israel/ethnic people to the faithful inward subset whose praise is from God
boundary_disagreement: Consensus separates a privileged symbolic inward reading from a dominant literal ethnic sense (plus contested transfers to church or remnant); the book unifies all as contextual scales of a single ‘belonging to Judah’ without a primary-symbolic vs. literal hierarchy.
material_contradiction: None; the book retains both the ethnic and the Rom 2 inward senses without denying either.
rationale: Minimum cores overlap on the ethnic people and the faithful inward subset (explicitly tied to praise-from-God language). The book preserves those referents but reorganizes them as multi-scalar extensions of ‘belonging to Judah’ determined by context, thereby broadening the identification and altering boundaries/precision relative to the consensus’s primary-symbolic-plus-alternatives structure. This is refinement of extension and framing, not replacement of the central referents.
strongest_objection: The book’s scalar framing may under-weight the contested supersessionist or church-as-true-Jew extensions that several consensus responses treat as common, or may appear too etymological/historical for a pure symbolism entry.
